medium.titulo: From claude -p to Published: How to Wire the Output Pipeline
medium.resumo: For builders who want Claude to write and post automatically — here is how the handoff from generation to publishing actually works.
medium.conteudo_html:
For builders who want Claude to write and post automatically — here is how the handoff from generation to publishing actually works.

This story was written with AI assistance.

Most builders hit the same wall. Claude writes something useful. Then they copy it, open a browser, log in, paste it, and click publish. Repeat across every platform, every day. That is not automation. That is just slower manual work with an AI in the middle.

The hard part of building a posting agent is not the writing. It is the handoff: getting the output out of Claude and into the publishing layer without a human touching anything. Get that right and the rest is a scheduler.

This is how I wired that pipeline for Brand Autopilot, the background agent I built to post to X, Reddit and Medium on a schedule. The pieces: claude -p for generation, Node.js for routing, Playwright for the browser.

Why the Output Format Is the Foundation

When you run claude -p and ask for a post, you get prose. That works for one platform. For a system that handles multiple platforms with different fields and formatting rules, prose becomes a parsing problem you do not want to solve.

Ask Claude to respond with a JSON object in a fixed schema instead. Something like platform, kind, and body as a minimum, with title added for platforms that need one. Every run outputs one object. Node.js reads it. The routing layer does not need to understand what Claude wrote, only what to do with the fields it finds.

Keep the schema minimal. Add a field only when a downstream step actually needs it. A platform field and a body field will carry you further than a twelve-field schema you built speculatively.

Getting Structured JSON Out of claude -p

claude -p runs Claude Code with a prompt passed as an argument and writes the result to stdout. That alone makes it scriptable from any environment that can run a shell command. The trick is in how you close the prompt.

End it with a strict instruction: reply with ONLY a JSON object, no text before or after it. Then include a concrete schema example directly in the prompt. Claude follows the shape consistently when the example is specific and the closing instruction is unambiguous. A schema example with two or three populated fields is more reliable than a prose description of what you want.

In Node.js, the pattern is: spawn claude as a child process with the prompt as an argument, capture stdout, then call JSON.parse on the trimmed result. If JSON.parse throws, Claude deviated from the schema. Log the raw output and exit cleanly. Do not try to salvage or patch malformed output. Treat the run as a failed attempt and let the scheduler trigger the next one.

Before wiring this to a scheduler, verify two things on your machine: that the claude binary is on your PATH, and that it is already authenticated. Brand Autopilot uses a normal Claude subscription login, not an API key. The binary needs to be set up and signed in before any scheduled call can succeed.

Routing in Node.js

Once you have a valid parsed object, routing is a map of platform name to handler function. Each handler receives the object and calls the right Playwright function for that platform.

Validate the object before routing. Check that all required fields are present and non-empty. Check that the platform value matches a handler you have registered. If anything fails, log the specific issue and exit with a non-zero code. A silent failure that produces no output is harder to debug than a script that exits loudly with a reason.

Pull configuration at this point too, not inside the individual handlers. Daily post limits, minimum gaps between posts, and quiet hours should live in a config.json file that the routing layer reads on each run. If you want to change the daily cap from 3 to 2, you edit a number in a file. You do not touch logic, and you do not redeploy anything.

Publishing With Playwright and a Saved Profile

Playwright is a browser automation library that drives a real Chromium, Firefox or WebKit install. For publishing to platforms that require a login, one detail matters more than anything else: use a saved browser profile from a real session, not a fresh headless instance.

A fresh browser has no cookies, no history, no persistent state. Platforms read those signals. A fresh instance looks like a bot. Google blocks sign-in entirely inside automation-controlled browsers, which breaks any platform that uses Google for authentication. The same pattern trips login detection on other platforms too.

The fix: log in once through a normal browser window. Then point Playwright to that profile's data directory when it launches. On each run, Playwright opens with the saved profile, the session cookies are already present, and the platform sees a returning user. This is the approach Brand Autopilot uses.

Keep each platform's handler short and specific. The page structure and publish flow differ across X, Reddit and Medium. Three separate functions are easier to maintain than a shared abstraction that breaks when one platform updates its layout and silently affects the others.

Enforcing Limits Inside the Script

The scheduler controls when the script fires. The script controls whether it does anything when it runs. These are two separate responsibilities, and mixing them is where agents go wrong.

At the top of every run, before calling claude -p, check three things: whether you are inside the quiet hours window, whether the minimum gap since the last post on this platform has elapsed, and whether the daily post count for this platform is below the limit. If any check fails, exit immediately. Nothing gets generated, nothing gets published.

Store the per-platform state, last post timestamp and today's count, in a file the script writes to after each successful publish. On the next run, it reads that file first. This keeps the state outside the scheduler and outside the script logic, which means you can inspect it, reset it manually, or back it up independently.

Run a Dry Run Before Going Live

Before the first scheduled run that actually publishes, run the script in a mode that generates and validates but does not call the Playwright publish function. Confirm the JSON comes back in the right shape. Confirm the routing picks the right handler. Confirm the config checks fire correctly.

Do this for each new platform you add. The first live run should be boring: you already know the JSON is valid, the handler navigates correctly, and the limits behave as expected. The surprises should happen in dry runs, not in production at 2am.

Start With One Platform

Wire the pipeline for X, or Reddit, or Medium. Not all three at once. Make sure claude -p returns clean JSON. Make sure the handler navigates and publishes. Make sure the limits stop a run when they should.

Once one platform is working end-to-end, the pattern repeats for the next. Add a handler, add an entry in the config, extend the prompt schema with any new fields.

The agent is not finished when the first post goes out. It is finished when it fails cleanly, logs why, and you notice without anything breaking in production.

The next step: run claude -p with a prompt that ends in a strict JSON instruction and parse the result with JSON.parse. If that works, the rest of the pipeline is plumbing.

medium.titulo: How Claude's Cheaper Model Ends Up Costing 24% More
medium.conteudo_html:
​

On Vals AI’s tax benchmark, Claude Opus 5.5 charges 60% less per output token than Fable 5.1, yet costs 24% more for every task it gets right. It thinks 4.5x as much. A short Python script checks your own runs.

Claude Opus 5.5 costs 60% less per output token than Claude Fable 5.1, but on Vals AI’s Tax Agent Bench it costs 24% more for every task it actually solves. Here’s why, and a script that runs the same check on your own API logs in five minutes.

01 — Where this comes from

On October 30 the AI Engineer YouTube channel posted “The Cheaper AI Model That Costs You More”, a 15-minute talk by Rayan Krishnan of Vals AI, a company that builds AI benchmarks.

Paraphrasing the auto-generated captions: on paper Opus 5.5 is cheaper than Fable 5.1, at $4 in and $20 out per million tokens against $10 and $50. On Vals’ tax benchmark it came out about 14% more expensive and scored lower (he says 3%; the leaderboard gap is 3.6 points), because the less capable model spends more tokens to get the work done.

Tokens are the word-pieces an API bills by. Here is the mechanism.

02 — The numbers, from the leaderboard

The Tax Agent Bench page (updated October 29) lists accuracy, the share of tasks a model got right, and average cost per task. Each model’s token count also opens a breakdown: input, cache writes, cache reads, output and reasoning.

+-------------------+--------+---------------+
| model             | score  | cost per task |
+===================+========+===============+
| Claude Fable 5.1  | 49.19% | $13.18        |
| Claude Opus 5.5   | 45.57% | $15.09        |
| Claude Opus 5     | 45.55% | $5.14         |
| Claude Sonnet 5.5 | 41.96% | $9.25         |
+-------------------+--------+---------------+

Cost divided by accuracy is the cost of one solved task. Fable 5.1 pays $26.79. Opus 5.5 pays $33.11, 24% more, for a model that is cheaper on every line of Anthropic’s price list.

03 — Where the money goes: thinking

Anthropic bills four kinds of tokens: fresh input, cache writes (saving a prompt prefix for reuse), cache reads (reusing it), and output. Output includes the model’s thinking tokens, billed at the output rate even when you only see a summary of them.​

Per task, Opus 5.5 produced 404k reasoning tokens. Fable 5.1 produced 90k, so Opus 5.5 thought 4.5 times as much. Visible output was about the same (59k against 57k), so nearly all of the 3.2x gap in total output is thinking. At list prices, output is 65% of Opus 5.5’s bill.

04 — The break-even rule

Opus 5.5’s output price is 0.4 times Fable 5.1’s, so it only saves money on output while it writes less than 2.5 times as many output tokens. It wrote 3.2 times as many and paid 27% more for output.

The other lines split. Cache writes went Opus 5.5’s way: 2.0 times the tokens at 0.4 times the price is 19% cheaper. Cache reads went against it: they’re only 20% cheaper per token ($0.20 against $0.25 per million), and it read 1.8 times as many, so it paid 44% more there.

Price per token is half the equation. No price list shows the other half: tokens per task.

05 — The script

costcheck.py uses only the Python standard library. It holds Anthropic's list prices (read October 31) and Vals' per-task token averages. It prices each bill line and works out the cost per solved task.​

"""costcheck.py - what does one SOLVED task cost on each Claude model?
  python3 costcheck.py                 # Vals AI Tax Agent Bench, 10/29/2026
  python3 costcheck.py my_runs.jsonl   # your own API usage logs
  PAIR="Claude Opus 5.5,Claude Fable 5.1" python3 costcheck.py
"""
import json, os, sys
# $ per million tokens: input, output, 5-min cache write, cache hit.
# Source: Anthropic pricing page, read 2026-10-31.
PRICE = {
    "Claude Fable 5.1":  (10.0, 50.0, 12.50, 0.25),
    "Claude Opus 5.5":   (4.0, 20.0, 5.00, 0.20),
    "Claude Opus 5":     (5.0, 25.0, 6.25, 0.50),
    "Claude Sonnet 5.5": (2.0, 10.0, 2.50, 0.10),
}
# Vals AI Tax Agent Bench (10/29/2026), per task: input, cache read,
# cache write, output incl. reasoning, reasoning; accuracy; Vals' cost.
VALS = {
    "Claude Fable 5.1":  (139, 1.90e6, 431.14e3, 146.31e3, 89.79e3,
                          0.4919, 13.18),
    "Claude Opus 5.5":   (223, 3.42e6, 875.16e3, 463.16e3, 403.70e3,
                          0.4557, 15.09),
    "Claude Opus 5":     (145, 1.30e6, 370.49e3, 86.85e3, 36.30e3,
                          0.4555, 5.14),
    "Claude Sonnet 5.5": (274, 5.00e6, 1.03e6, 565.60e3, 493.19e3,
                          0.4196, 9.25),
}
def lines(model, inp, hit, write, out):
    """Dollars per bill line: input, cache hits, cache writes, output."""
    p_in, p_out, p_w, p_hit = PRICE[model]
    return [inp * p_in / 1e6, hit * p_hit / 1e6,
            write * p_w / 1e6, out * p_out / 1e6]
def cost(model, inp, hit, write, out):
    return sum(lines(model, inp, hit, write, out))
def name(model_id):
    """Accept "Claude Opus 5.5" or an API id like "claude-opus-5-5"."""
    for m in PRICE:
        if model_id.lower().replace("-", " ") in (
                m.lower(), m.lower().replace(".", " ")):
            return m
    sys.exit(f"unknown model {model_id!r}: add it to PRICE")
def from_logs(path):
    """One JSON object per line: {"model", "usage", "passed"}.
    usage holds the Messages API fields input_tokens, output_tokens,
    cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens."""
    runs = {}
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            if not line.strip():
                continue
            r = json.loads(line)
            u = r["usage"]
            m = name(r["model"])
            c = cost(m, u.get("input_tokens") or 0,
                     u.get("cache_read_input_tokens") or 0,
                     u.get("cache_creation_input_tokens") or 0,
                     u.get("output_tokens") or 0)
            s = runs.setdefault(m, [0, 0, 0.0])
            s[0] += 1
            s[1] += bool(r["passed"])
            s[2] += c
    return runs
def main():
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        if not os.path.isfile(sys.argv[1]):
            print("usage: python3 costcheck.py [runs.jsonl]")
            sys.exit(1)
        print(f"{'model':18} {'tasks':>5} {'solved':>6} "
              f"{'$ total':>8} {'$/solved':>9}")
        for m, (n, ok, usd) in from_logs(sys.argv[1]).items():
            per = f"{usd / ok:9.2f}" if ok else "      n/a"
            print(f"{m:18} {n:5d} {ok:6d} {usd:8.2f} {per}")
        return
    print("basis: Vals AI Tax Agent Bench averages x Anthropic list prices")
    print(f"{'model':18} {'list $':>7} {'Vals $':>7} {'gap':>5} "
          f"{'think':>6} {'score':>6} {'$/solved':>9}")
    rows = {}
    for m, (inp, hit, write, out, think, acc, vals) in VALS.items():
        mine = cost(m, inp, hit, write, out)
        per = vals / acc  # Vals' cost / accuracy = $ per solved task
        rows[m] = (inp, hit, write, out, think, acc, vals, per)
        print(f"{m:18} {mine:7.2f} {vals:7.2f} "
              f"{round((mine / vals - 1) * 100):+4d}% {think / 1e3:5.0f}k "
              f"{acc * 100:5.1f}% {per:9.2f}")
    pair = os.environ.get("PAIR", "Claude Opus 5.5,Claude Fable 5.1")
    a, b = [name(x.strip()) for x in pair.split(",")]
    ra, rb = rows[a], rows[b]
    la, lb = lines(a, *ra[:4]), lines(b, *rb[:4])
    print(f"\n{a} vs {b}  (ratios are first / second)")
    print(f"  output price ratio  : {PRICE[a][1] / PRICE[b][1]:.2f}x")
    print(f"  output tokens ratio : {ra[3] / rb[3]:.2f}x")
    print(f"  reasoning ratio     : {ra[4] / rb[4]:.2f}x")
    for i, label in [(3, "output"), (2, "cache writes"), (1, "cache hits")]:
        print(f"  {label + ' $':20}: {la[i]:5.2f} vs {lb[i]:5.2f} "
              f"({la[i] / lb[i] - 1:+.0%})")
    print(f"  output share of bill: {la[3] / sum(la):.0%} vs "
          f"{lb[3] / sum(lb):.0%}")
    print(f"  cost per task       : {ra[6] / rb[6] - 1:+.0%}")
    print(f"  cost per solved task: {ra[7] / rb[7] - 1:+.0%}")
    be = PRICE[b][1] / PRICE[a][1]
    print(f"  break-even output   : {be:.2f}x the tokens "
          f"(above it, {a} pays more)")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

​

06 — What it prints

$ python3 costcheck.py
basis: Vals AI Tax Agent Bench averages x Anthropic list prices
model               list $  Vals $   gap  think  score  $/solved
Claude Fable 5.1     13.18   13.18   +0%    90k  49.2%     26.79
Claude Opus 5.5      14.32   15.09   -5%   404k  45.6%     33.11
Claude Opus 5         5.14    5.14   +0%    36k  45.6%     11.28
Claude Sonnet 5.5     8.73    9.25   -6%   493k  42.0%     22.04
Claude Opus 5.5 vs Claude Fable 5.1  (ratios are first / second)
  output price ratio  : 0.40x
  output tokens ratio : 3.17x
  reasoning ratio     : 4.50x
  output $            :  9.26 vs  7.32 (+27%)
  cache writes $      :  4.38 vs  5.39 (-19%)
  cache hits $        :  0.68 vs  0.47 (+44%)
  output share of bill: 65% vs 55%
  cost per task       : +14%
  cost per solved task: +24%
  break-even output   : 2.50x the tokens (above it, Claude Opus 5.5 pays more)

“list $” is my recomputation. It matches Vals to the cent for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5, and runs 5–6% low for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5; the page doesn’t say why. On both numbers Opus 5.5 costs more per task than Fable 5.1. The $/solved column uses Vals' own cost, not mine.

07 — Run it on your own logs

Every Claude Messages API response carries a usage object with input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens. Save it with the model and whether the task passed your own check, one JSON object per line. The model can be the API id, such as claude-opus-5-5 (no date suffix).

This writes four made-up runs in that format:

# Writes toy.jsonl: four made-up runs in the shape costcheck.py reads.
import json
RUNS = [  # model, passed, input, cache read, cache write, output
    ("claude-opus-5-5", True, 1200, 90000, 20000, 14000),
    ("Claude Opus 5.5", False, 1500, 120000, 25000, 21000),
    ("Claude Fable 5.1", True, 1200, 60000, 18000, 5000),
    ("Claude Fable 5.1", True, 1300, 70000, 19000, 6000),
]
with open("toy.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for model, ok, i, hit, w, out in RUNS:
        usage = {"input_tokens": i, "cache_read_input_tokens": hit,
                 "cache_creation_input_tokens": w, "output_tokens": out}
        f.write(json.dumps({"model": model, "passed": ok,
                            "usage": usage}) + "\n")

​

$ python3 make_toy.py && python3 costcheck.py toy.jsonl
model              tasks solved  $ total  $/solved
Claude Opus 5.5        2      1     0.98      0.98
Claude Fable 5.1       2      2     1.07      0.53

Toy numbers, not measurements. A missing file exits with a usage line; an unknown model asks you to add it to PRICE. Cache writes use the 5-minute rate; if you use 1-hour caching, put the 1-hour rate in PRICE.

08 — The one setting to change: PAIR

PAIR is an environment variable naming two models. The first is the one being judged, and every ratio is first divided by second. Try Opus 5.5 against the previous Opus:

$ PAIR="Claude Opus 5,Claude Opus 5.5" python3 costcheck.py | tail -11
Claude Opus 5 vs Claude Opus 5.5  (ratios are first / second)
  output price ratio  : 1.25x
  output tokens ratio : 0.19x
  reasoning ratio     : 0.09x
  output $            :  2.17 vs  9.26 (-77%)
  cache writes $      :  2.32 vs  4.38 (-47%)
  cache hits $        :  0.65 vs  0.68 (-5%)
  output share of bill: 42% vs 65%
  cost per task       : -66%
  cost per solved task: -66%
  break-even output   : 0.80x the tokens (above it, Claude Opus 5 pays more)

Opus 5 lists higher than Opus 5.5 on every line ($25 against $20 for output) and scored 45.55% against 45.57%. But it reasoned about a tenth as much, so each task cost 66% less.

09 — What this doesn’t tell you

  • One benchmark. Krishnan’s point is that the best model changes by task.
  • Effort. Vals ran Opus 5.5 at max effort by default, and its effort chart shows the score falling at lower settings. Anthropic's API default for Opus 5.5 is medium, so your runs may already think less than the benchmark did. Test effort before switching models.

The scores, costs and token counts are Vals’ measurements; the prices are Anthropic’s. Everything computed from them in sections 02–08 (cost per solved task, recomputed bills, ratios, shares and break-even) is printed by costcheck.py, except the per-line token and price ratios in section 04, worked out from its tables. Nothing here was run against the Claude API.​

10 — Verdict

On Vals’ tax benchmark, Claude Opus 5.5 is cheaper per token than Fable 5.1 but 24% more expensive per solved task. It writes 3.2 times the output, thinks 4.5 times as much and solves fewer tasks. Log usage and pass/fail for a day, run the script, and choose on cost per solved task, not price per token.

Have you ever switched to a cheaper model and watched the bill go up?

If this saves you a bad model switch, a clap helps others find it.

Follow me for daily LLM deep-dives.

medium.resumo: System Scaling: Understanding the Challenges and Strategies
medium.conteudo_html:
System Scaling: Understanding the Challenges and Strategies

At the beginning of a project, you don’t need a complex infrastructure. A single server might be enough to run your application and serve users efficiently.

But as the number of users and incoming requests increases, an important question starts to appear:

How can we make the system handle more load without affecting performance or losing control of infrastructure costs?

This is where Scaling comes into play.

Scaling is the ability of a system to handle an increasing workload, either by increasing the resources of existing machines or by adding new machines to distribute the load.

But before exploring scaling strategies, we need to understand the challenges that come with system growth.

1. Latency

Latency is the time it takes for a system to process a request and return a response.

Imagine you have a page that needs to call five services sequentially, not in parallel, where each service must wait for the previous one to finish.

If each service takes 200ms, the total delay could reach one full second, excluding network overhead and additional operations.

The problem here is that latency accumulates with every sequential operation.

2. Bottlenecks

A bottleneck is a component that limits the performance of the entire system, even when other components have enough available resources.

Imagine you have 100 Application Servers, and all of them are sending queries to a single Database.

You can keep adding more Application Servers, but if the Database cannot handle the additional workload, the overall system performance will remain limited by the Database’s capacity.

Adding more resources doesn’t always mean better performance.

You must first identify the component that prevents the system from handling more load.

3. Downtime

As infrastructure grows, managing failures becomes more complicated.

A server might crash, a network connection might fail, or a database might become unavailable.

The goal is not to prevent every possible failure, but to design the system so it can handle failures and continue providing services whenever possible.

This brings us to two important concepts: High Availability and Fault Tolerance.

4. Cost

Scaling is not just about adding servers. It’s also about managing infrastructure costs.

There are two common problems:

  • Over-provisioning: Allocating more resources than you actually need, which means paying for resources you’re not using.
  • Uncontrolled Autoscaling: Allowing the system to automatically add servers without proper limits, which can lead to unexpectedly high cloud bills.

The goal is not to achieve maximum performance at any cost, but to maintain a balance between Performance and Cost.

Second: Scaling Strategies

1. Vertical Scaling

Instead of adding a new server, you increase the resources of the existing server.

You can upgrade:

  • CPU Cores
  • RAM
  • Storage Capacity

Advantages:

  • Easy to implement.
  • Usually doesn’t require major changes to the Application Architecture.
  • Suitable for small projects and MVPs.

Disadvantages:

  • Hardware Limit: You cannot increase resources indefinitely.
  • Can become very expensive when upgrading to high-end machines.
  • May introduce a Single Point of Failure, because if the server goes down, the entire application might become unavailable if there is no backup.

Think of it this way: instead of buying another car, you buy a bigger car that can carry more passengers.

2. Horizontal Scaling

Instead of increasing the resources of a single server, you add more servers to share the workload.

For example, instead of running your application on one server, you deploy it across five servers and use a Load Balancer to distribute incoming requests between them.

The Load Balancer receives requests and forwards them to available servers.

Advantages:

  • You can increase the number of servers based on demand.
  • Helps improve Availability.
  • If one server goes down, the remaining servers can continue handling requests.

Challenges:

  • Requires a Load Balancer.
  • Requires a Stateless Application Design.
  • Requires handling Shared State and Session Management.
  • Increases architectural complexity.
  • May require Database Replication and Distributed Caching.

3. Diagonal Scaling

Diagonal Scaling combines Vertical and Horizontal Scaling.

The idea is to start by upgrading the resources of your existing server. Once you reach a certain limit, you start adding more servers.

For example:

  1. Start with a server that has 4 CPU Cores and 8 GB RAM.
  2. As the load increases, upgrade it to 8 CPU Cores and 16 GB RAM.
  3. Once you reach the server’s practical limits, add more servers.
  4. Use a Load Balancer to distribute the workload.

This way, you benefit from the simplicity of Vertical Scaling at the beginning and the flexibility of Horizontal Scaling as your system grows.

Third: Comparing Scaling Strategies

Each strategy has its own use cases and advantages:

  • Vertical Scaling: Easier to implement and less complex, but limited by the machine’s capacity.
  • Horizontal Scaling: More flexible and scalable, but requires a more complex architecture and management of multiple servers.
  • Diagonal Scaling: Combines the simplicity of Vertical Scaling with the flexibility of Horizontal Scaling, making it suitable for applications that grow gradually.

Note: There is no single best strategy for every situation. The right choice depends on the application’s nature, workload, budget, and availability requirements.

使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫

最近在處理 Nuxt 網站的安全性設定時

Nuxt 明明是前端框架

卻可以透過 server/middleware 修改伺服器回傳的 HTTP Header？

原來 Nuxt 不只是 Vue 的前端開發工具，它也具備伺服器端的執行能力

Nuxt 不只是前端框架

在一般 Vue SPA（Single Page Application）中

伺服器主要提供 HTML、CSS 和 JavaScript 檔案

瀏覽器下載後，再由 JavaScript 產生畫面

Nuxt 則支援 SSR（Server-Side Rendering，伺服器端渲染）。

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  ssr: true
})

當 SSR 啟用時

Nuxt 可以先在伺服器執行 Vue 程式、產生 HTML，再傳送給瀏覽器。

瀏覽器收到 HTML 後，會再透過 JavaScript 接手互動功能

這個過程稱為 Hydration。

因此 Nuxt 的程式可能在兩個不同環境執行：

  • Server（伺服器）：產生 HTML、處理 HTTP 請求。
  • Client（瀏覽器）：呈現畫面、處理使用者互動。

Nuxt 使用的伺服器引擎叫做 Nitro

它可以處理 SSR、Server API 和 Server Middleware。

Middleware 是什麼？

Middleware 中文稱為「中介軟體」。

可以把它想成辦公大樓的警衛。

當有人準備進入辦公室時，警衛會先檢查身分，確認符合條件才讓他進去。

Middleware 也是類似的概念

在主要處理流程之前，先執行某些工作。

Nuxt 有兩種容易搞混的 Middleware。

Route Middleware

放在：middleware/

主要處理頁面導航

例如檢查使用者是否登入。

export default defineNuxtRouteMiddleware((to) => {
  const isLoggedIn = false

  if (!isLoggedIn && to.path !== '/login') {
    return navigateTo('/login')
  }
})

Server Middleware

放在：server/middleware/

主要處理進入 Nitro 的 HTTP 請求

例如記錄請求資訊、設定 HTTP Response Header。

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(event, 'X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff')
})

兩者最大的差別是：

  • Route Middleware：處理使用者要前往哪個頁面。
  • Server Middleware：處理伺服器收到的 HTTP 請求。

為什麼需要 X-Content-Type-Options？

當瀏覽器向伺服器索取檔案時

伺服器會透過 Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器檔案類型。

Content-Type: text/html
Content-Type: application/javascript
Content-Type: text/css

但某些情況下，瀏覽器可能根據檔案內容自行猜測類型。

這種行為稱為 MIME Sniffing。

伺服器回傳：

Content-Type: text/plain

但檔案內容卻是：

alert("Hello!")

伺服器宣告這是普通文字，但內容看起來像 JavaScript。

如果瀏覽器在載入腳本時自行猜測類型並執行，就可能增加安全風險。

因此可以設定：

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

要求瀏覽器在載入 JavaScript、CSS 等資源時，遵守對應的 MIME 類型檢查。

如果宣告的類型不符合要求，瀏覽器就會阻擋載入，而不是自行猜測後繼續使用。

使用 Server Middleware 設定安全標頭

在 Nuxt 專案建立：

server/middleware/security-headers.ts

import {
  defineEventHandler,
  setResponseHeader
} from 'h3'

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(
    event,
    'X-Content-Type-Options',
    'nosniff'
  )
})

這段程式其實只做一件事情：

在 Nuxt 伺服器處理 HTTP 請求時，替回應加入 X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff。

逐行來看：

  • defineEventHandler()：建立一個 HTTP 請求處理函式。
  • event：代表這次 HTTP 請求與回應的相關資訊。
  • setResponseHeader()：替 HTTP 回應設定 Header。
  • X-Content-Type-Options：安全標頭名稱。
  • nosniff：要求瀏覽器遵守對應資源的 MIME 類型限制。

因為檔案放在 server/middleware/，Nuxt 會自動註冊這段程式。

不需要在每個 Vue 頁面重複設定。

不過要注意，這個 Middleware 只能影響經過 Nitro 處理的 HTTP 回應。

如果正式環境還有 IIS、Nginx 或其他 Web Server 直接提供檔案，就需要另外確認。

如何驗證設定成功？

啟動 Nuxt 專案後，可以使用 Chrome 開發者工具確認。

  1. 按下 F12 開啟 DevTools。
  2. 選擇 Network。
  3. 重新整理網頁。
  4. 點選網頁的 Document 請求。
  5. 查看 Response Headers。
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html;charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

這代表目前檢查的 HTTP 回應已經包含安全標頭。

另外，也應檢查 JavaScript 和 CSS 是否具有正確的 Content-Type

避免新增 nosniff 後造成檔案載入失敗。

重點整理

  • Nuxt 不只是前端工具，也具備透過 Nitro 執行伺服器端程式的能力。
  • SSR 可以在伺服器先產生 HTML，再交由瀏覽器接手互動。
  • Route Middleware 負責頁面導航與路由檢查。
  • Server Middleware 負責 Nuxt 伺服器端的 HTTP 請求處理。
  • Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器回應內容的類型。
  • MIME Sniffing 是瀏覽器根據內容自行判斷檔案類型的行為。
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff 可以降低特定資源因 MIME 類型錯誤判斷而產生的安全風險。
  • 設定完成後，仍需要檢查 HTTP 回應，確認標頭確實生效。

medium.titulo: Why Do We Even Need React, Vue and Angular? 6 Things They Do So You Don’t Have To
medium.resumo: In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself.
medium.conteudo_html:
In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself. What they add is knowing when to call them, which ones to use, and which calls to skip.

Open the source of React, Vue or Angular and you won’t find any browser magic. They create elements with document.createElement, change text with nodeValue and textContent, and attach listeners with addEventListener, exactly like you would in a plain .js file.

So why does almost every team reach for one of them? It isn’t because the DOM is slow or because vanilla JavaScript can’t build a real app. These libraries make a long list of small decisions for you, on every click, and they get them right every time. You would get most of them right too, at least on the first day. By month six, with three teammates and forty screens, you’d be getting them wrong.

Here are the six that matter most. I checked each one against the shipped source of React 19.3, Vue 3.5 and Angular 21.2, and measured the browser side in Chrome 156. The interactive version of this post, with live demos you can run in your browser, is on allahabadi.dev.

1. You stop updating the screen by hand

This is the big one, and every other point in this post sits on top of it.

Take a small shopping cart. A cart icon shows a count, a list shows the items, a line shows the total, and the checkout button says how many items you’re buying. Four places on the screen show the same piece of data.

Without a library, every action has to remember every place:

<span id="badge">0</span>
<ul id="list"></ul>
<b id="total">0</b>
<button id="checkout">Checkout (0)</button>
const cart = [];
const badge = document.querySelector('#badge');
const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const total = document.querySelector('#total');
const checkout = document.querySelector('#checkout');
function addItem(item) {
  cart.push(item);
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = `${item.name} ₹${item.price}`;
  list.append(li);
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function removeLast() {
  cart.pop();
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.lastElementChild?.remove();
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  // checkout.textContent was never updated here
}

Nothing in that code crashes. removeLast just forgets the checkout button, so after you remove an item the button still says the old number. No error shows up in the console, and no test fails unless someone wrote one for that exact label. A real app has hundreds of these "update these four things" functions, and each new feature adds one more place each of them has to remember.

The fix is to flip the direction. Instead of writing “when this happens, change these elements”, you write one function that says what the screen should look like for any cart, and you call it after every change:

let cart = [];
function render() {
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.replaceChildren(...cart.map((i) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `${i.name} ₹${i.price}`;
    return li;
  }));
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function addItem(item) { cart = [...cart, item]; render(); }
function removeLast() { cart = cart.slice(0, -1); render(); }

(It uses the same four const elements as the first snippet.) Now no action can forget the button, because no action touches the screen at all. They change the data, and render draws the screen from it. People describe this as UI is a function of state: same state in, same screen out.

That is the whole idea React, Vue and Angular are built on. In React the same cart looks like this:

import { useState } from 'react';
export function Cart() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);
  const total = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  return (
    <>
      <span>{cart.length}</span>
      <ul>
        {cart.map((i, n) => <li key={n}>{i.name} ₹{i.price}</li>)}
      </ul>
      <b>{total}</b>
      <button onClick={() => setCart([...cart, { name: 'Tea', price: 40 }])}>Add tea</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCart(cart.slice(0, -1))}>Remove last</button>
      <button>Checkout ({cart.length})</button>
    </>
  );
}

But my vanilla render() has a cost the React version doesn't. It rebuilds the whole list on every click, even when only one item changed. Do that on a list of 2,000 rows and the browser throws away 2,000 elements and builds 2,000 new ones to change one price. Doing "render from state" without paying that price is the actual work these libraries do, and the next three sections are about how they do it.

2. They pick the right moment to touch the DOM

A browser tab runs your JavaScript and draws the page on the same thread. It can’t paint while your code is running. Roughly, one turn of the loop looks like this: run a task (your click handler), run the microtasks queued during it, run requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then recalculate styles, lay the page out and paint.

When you change the DOM directly, the change happens right there, in the middle of your handler. When you then read something that depends on layout (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), innerText), the browser has to stop and lay the page out right now, because the layout it has is out of date. Do that in a loop and you get one full layout per pass. This has a name: layout thrashing.

const rows = document.querySelectorAll('.row');
const heights = [];
for (const row of rows) {
  row.textContent = 'Read';        // write: layout is now out of date
  heights.push(row.offsetHeight);  // read: browser must lay out right now
}

The libraries never write to the DOM the moment you change state. They write it down and do all the DOM work later, in one go:

  • React collects every setState call made during an event. If your click handler calls setName, setCity and setAge, React renders once and commits once, after your handler returns and before the browser paints. Work that isn't urgent, like a startTransition update, goes through React's scheduler, which posts its work with MessageChannel and gives the main thread back every 5 ms so a keypress doesn't have to wait for a long render.
  • Vue puts each component that needs updating in a queue and flushes the whole queue in one microtask (Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs)). That is why you need await nextTick() to see the updated DOM right after changing state.
  • Angular in zoneless mode schedules change detection with whichever fires first, a setTimeout or a requestAnimationFrame, so a burst of changes in one handler leads to one check.

The core of the trick fits in six lines:

let queued = false;
function scheduleRender(render) {
  if (queued) return;
  queued = true;
  queueMicrotask(() => { queued = false; render(); });
}

Call scheduleRender(render) ten times in one click and render runs once.

One correction to something you’ll often read: none of the three uses requestIdleCallback to apply your updates. An idle callback can be delayed for a long time, and an update needs to be on screen in the next frame. Vue uses it for hydrateOnIdle, and Angular for @defer (on idle) blocks. Both are cases where waiting is fine.

You can do all of this by hand. You’d have to know that layout reads in a loop are expensive, that a microtask runs before the next paint, and that requestAnimationFrame exists. Then you'd have to make sure every developer on the team knows it as well, in every file.

3. They choose the fast DOM API for you

The DOM often gives you two ways to do the same thing, and one of them costs a lot more. The best-known pair is textContent and innerText.

textContent joins up the text nodes inside an element. It never looks at CSS. innerText returns the text as it appears on screen: it leaves out elements hidden with CSS, applies text-transform, and turns line boxes into line breaks. To know what is on screen, the browser needs up-to-date styles and layout. So reading innerText right after you changed something forces a full layout.

Writing is a different story, and this is where the usual advice gets it half wrong. In my traces, setting innerText did not force layout. It cost about the same as setting textContent. The only difference is that the innerText setter turns \n into <br> elements. The expensive part is reading it.

The read is easy to put in a hot loop without noticing, like this search filter:

const query = 'error';
for (const row of document.querySelectorAll('.row')) {
  row.hidden = !row.innerText.includes(query);
}

Setting row.hidden makes the layout out of date, and the next row's innerText needs it to be current, so the browser lays the page out again for every row. Swap innerText for textContent and that loop doesn't do any layout until the frame is painted.

Here is how React sets text on an element, from react-dom 19.3 (lightly reformatted):

function setTextContent(node, text) {
  if (text) {
    var firstChild = node.firstChild;
    if (firstChild && firstChild === node.lastChild && 3 === firstChild.nodeType) {
      firstChild.nodeValue = text;
      return;
    }
  }
  node.textContent = text;
}

If the element already holds exactly one text node, React changes that node’s nodeValue in place, which is the cheapest text write the DOM has. Otherwise it uses textContent. innerText doesn't appear anywhere in that path.

Most of the time, these libraries don’t read the DOM at all. The current cart, the current name and the current filter all live in JavaScript, in React’s fibers, Vue’s reactive objects or Angular’s views. When your code reads row.innerText to find out what a row says, it asks the browser to work it out from the page. A library already knows, because it rendered that row. Fewer reads means fewer chances to force layout, and you don't need to remember which layout-reading APIs are dangerous. I measured more than 40 of them in another post.

They skip updates that change nothing

Say a price on the screen is 499, and your code sets it to 499 again. Nothing on screen changes. Does the browser notice?

I tested it in Chrome 156 on a page with 3,000 paragraphs. Each test wrote the same value 200 times and read offsetWidth after each write, the way real code often measures right after updating:

  • el.textContent = '499' (same value): 200 layouts. textContent replaces the child text node with a brand new one every time, so the browser treats it as new content.
  • el.innerHTML = '499' (same value): 200 layouts, for the same reason, plus an HTML parse each time.
  • textNode.nodeValue = '499' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome sees that nothing changed. A MutationObserver still received all 200 records, though.
  • el.style.width = '50px' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome skips an identical inline style too.
  • if (el.textContent !== '499') el.textContent = '499': 0 layouts, 0 mutations.

So the browser skips some identical writes and redoes others, and the two most common ways of setting text are the ones it redoes. You’d have to know which is which.

const price = document.querySelector('#price');
for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
  price.textContent = '499';
  price.offsetWidth;
}

All three libraries put the check in front of the DOM, so they never need that list:

  • React compares old and new text before it marks a text node for update (current.memoizedProps !== newProps). One level up, if you call setCount(5) while the count is already 5, Object.is says nothing changed and React can skip rendering that component altogether.
  • Vue’s reactive setter runs hasChanged(value, oldValue) first. Assigning the same value to a ref doesn't trigger anything that depends on it.
  • Angular compares every template binding to its previous value with Object.is (bindingUpdated) and only touches the DOM when it differs.

All three compare with Object.is, so they check "is it the same value", not "does it look the same":

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
Object.is(user, user);              // true:  update skipped
Object.is(user, { name: 'Asha' });  // false: treated as a change

That is why in React you create a new object to trigger an update, and why a new object built on every render can cause updates you didn’t expect.

5. They treat text as text

This is the reason I’d add to the list. It saves teams from a whole class of security bugs without anyone thinking about it.

When you build UI by hand, the quick way to put a value into a page is innerHTML. It parses whatever string you give it as HTML. If that string came from a user, the user can write HTML into your page, including elements with event handlers that run their JavaScript under your domain. That attack is called cross-site scripting, or XSS.

const greeting = document.querySelector('#greeting');
const name = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('name') ?? '';
greeting.innerHTML = `Hi ${name}`;    // parses name as HTML
greeting.textContent = `Hi ${name}`;  // shows name as plain text

In React, <p>Hi {name}</p> always produces a text node, whatever name holds. Vue's {{ name }} and Angular's {{ name }} work the same way. To put raw HTML on the page you have to ask for it by name: React calls it dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Vue calls it v-html, and Angular runs anything bound to [innerHTML] through its sanitizer first. The safe way is the default, and the unsafe way is the one you have to go looking for.

6. They make a big codebase easier to work in

The first five points are things the library does at runtime. This one is about the people writing the code, and on a large team it may matter most of all.

  • Components. A <PriceTag> is written once, used in forty places, and changed in one file. With plain DOM code, "reuse" usually means copying a function and its HTML string into another file.
  • Clean-up has a home. Listeners you attach in the template (onClick, @click, (click)) are removed for you when the component goes away, and each library gives you one obvious place for the rest: the useEffect clean-up in React, onUnmounted in Vue, DestroyRef in Angular. By hand, every removeEventListener is yours to remember, and a forgotten one keeps the old element and everything it refers to in memory.
  • Tools that understand your app. React DevTools, Vue DevTools and Angular DevTools show your components and their current state, not just a tree of divs. Hot reload swaps an edited component while the page keeps running, often without losing what you typed into a form.
  • The editor catches mistakes. TypeScript checks JSX and Angular templates, so a misspelled prop or a wrong type shows up as you type, not as a blank screen.
  • A shared map. Routing, forms, data fetching and tests have well-known answers in each ecosystem. A new teammate who knows React already knows where state lives in your app and how a screen gets drawn. Hand-written DOM code is different in every company, and sometimes in every file.

When plain JavaScript is enough

None of this means every page needs a framework. This site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework at all. A blog post, a landing page, or a form with a couple of toggles has very little state and only a few places that show it, so the bugs from the first section rarely have room to happen.

A simple rule of thumb: reach for a library when the same data shows up in several parts of the screen and changes often. That’s where updating by hand starts to break, and where batching, skipping and safe defaults pay for the JavaScript you ship. Below that point, a few addEventListener calls and textContent are perfectly fine.

React, Vue and Angular are still DOM code. They call the same APIs you can. The difference is that they pick the moment, pick the cheap method, skip the pointless call and escape the dangerous string on every update, including the ones nobody on your team thought about.

All five demos (the two carts, the batching race, the innerText filter, the same-value counter and the innerHTML parser) run live here: https://allahabadi.dev/blogs/frontend/why-we-need-react-vue-angular/

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Em comemoração aos 30 anos da Velocità, Sérgio Rocha conversa com o sócio Alexandre Estefano sobre a história da loja, a evolução dos tênis, vestuário e nutrição, o fenômeno das crews de corrida, além de detalhes da Black Friday Run e do treinão de aniversário que conectará as 5…
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Sábado | 31 de outubro de 2026

Para comemorar os 30 anos da Velocità, a maior rede de lojas especializadas em corrida do Brasil, bati um papo com Alexandre Estefano, um dos sócios da marca. Ele contou que a loja começou em 1996, não como um negócio focado em corrida, mas como uma loja multiesportiva chamada All Sport. A transição para se especializar em corrida acompanhou a evolução do próprio esporte no país.

Nossa conversa passou por toda a transformação do mercado. Antigamente, a grande questão na hora de escolher um tênis era o tipo de pisada: pronada, supinada ou neutra. Hoje, com a revolução tecnológica, o foco mudou para as novas espumas, como o Boost da Adidas, que introduziu o conceito de responsividade, e, mais recentemente, as placas de carbono. Essa evolução, claro, veio acompanhada de um salto nos preços, com tênis chegando a custar mais de R$ 2 mil.

Também falamos sobre o crescimento de outras áreas do mercado. O segmento de nutrição esportiva explodiu, com muitas marcas brasileiras de qualidade surgindo, como a Forcecell, Dobro e Z2. O vestuário também passou por uma grande revolução, especialmente o feminino. O que antes era apenas short e regata, hoje tem uma variedade imensa de tops, bermudas e macaquinhos cheios de bolsos funcionais e com um apelo estético que valoriza o corpo da mulher.

Outro ponto que abordamos foi o fenômeno cultural das “crews de corrida”. Esses grupos, que surgiram de forma “underground”, têm uma filosofia de ocupar a cidade, correndo em locais e horários com menos movimento de carros. É um movimento que tem crescido e se profissionalizado, com alguns grupos enfrentando questões legais com prefeituras e federações por conta do tamanho que atingiram.

Alexandre também falou sobre as iniciativas da Velocità para se conectar com a comunidade. Uma delas é a famosa Black Friday Run, uma promoção que já existe há 10 anos, onde o corredor acumula descontos ao registrar seus quilômetros corridos. A ideia é que o atleta conquiste o desconto fazendo o que mais gosta: correr. Outra novidade é o Clube Velocità, que integra os dados do Strava e Garmin para dar pontos aos corredores por suas corridas, que podem ser trocados por descontos.

Para celebrar o aniversário de 30 anos, a Velocità vai organizar um treinão especial que conectará as cinco lojas da rede em São Paulo. O percurso mais longo terá 37 km, saindo da Zona Leste, e haverá pelotões começando em outras lojas para percursos de 22 km, 12 km e 7 km. Todos os grupos se encontrarão na loja de Moema para a festa de comemoração.
